title: ZIF-derived bifunctional Cu@CueNeC composite electrocatalysts towards efficient electroreduction of oxygen and carbon dioxide
abstract: A Cu@CueNeC composite electrocatalyst with metallic Cu NPs and Cu(II)-Nx species embedded into the carbon matrix was pyrolyzed from ZIF-8 precursor through the formation of Cu(OH)2@ZIF-8. The optimal Cu@CueNeC catalyst obtained at 1000 C features a hollow polyhedral morphology, which is resulted from the carbothermal reaction of in-situ generated Cu2O and ZnO with carbon beyond 800 C. The bestperformance Cu@CueNeC exhibits an impressive catalytic bifunction towards oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) and carbon dioxide reduction (CO2RR) which is assumed to be imparted by the unique Cu(0)Cu(II)-Nx active sites. In alkaline electrolyte, it shows the ORR performance (E1/21⁄4 0.83 V vs RHE) comparable to Pt/C (E1/21⁄4 0.85 V vs RHE), and the assembled zinc-air (Zn-air) battery displays an excellent durability with the open circuit voltage (1.23 V) decaying only by ca. 4.2% in 80 h at 20mA cm 2. For CO2RR, it also delivers an outstanding catalytic performance converting CO2 into CO with a high Faradaic efficiency (90% at 0.5 V vs RHE). Control experiments have indicated that the potential synergistic interactions between Cu (0) (from Cu NPs) and Cu-Nx sites have promoting effects on both ORR and CO2RR. © 2019 Elsevier Ltd. A Cu@CueNeC composite electrocatalyst with metallic Cu NPs and Cu(II)-Nx species embedded into the carbon matrix was pyrolyzed from ZIF-8 precursor through the formation of Cu(OH)2@ZIF-8. The optimal Cu@CueNeC catalyst obtained at 1000 C features a hollow polyhedral morphology, which is resulted from the carbothermal reaction of in-situ generated Cu2O and ZnO with carbon beyond 800 C. The bestperformance Cu@CueNeC exhibits an impressive catalytic bifunction towards oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) and carbon dioxide reduction (CO2RR) which is assumed to be imparted by the unique Cu(0)Cu(II)-Nx active sites. In alkaline electrolyte, it shows the ORR performance (E1/2¼ 0.83 V vs RHE) comparable to Pt/C (E1/2¼ 0.85 V vs RHE), and the assembled zinc-air (Zn-air) battery displays an excellent durability with the open circuit voltage (1.23 V) decaying only by ca. 4.2% in 80 h at 20mA cm 2. For CO2RR, it also delivers an outstanding catalytic performance converting CO2 into CO with a high Faradaic efficiency (90% at 0.5 V vs RHE). Control experiments have indicated that the potential synergistic interactions between Cu (0) (from Cu NPs) and Cu-Nx sites have promoting effects on both ORR and CO2RR.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Over the past decade, transition-metal (M¼ Fe, Co, Ni etc.) and nitrogen (N) co-doped carbon (M/NeC) materials have been emerging as a class of versatile electrocatalysts towards a range of electrochemical reactions including oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) [1e5], oxygen evolution reaction (OER) [6e11], hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) [12e15] and carbon dioxide reduction reaction (CO2RR) [16e19], which generally play decisive roles in advanced techniques related to energy-conversion/storage and environmental issues. Generally, these promising M/NeC materials are prepared by pyrolyzing the suitable precursors under different atmospheres (e.g. N2, Ar2 and NH3 etc.). In this area, a variety of

precursors including inorganic/organic small molecules, organic polymers, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) and even biomass have been employed in order to engineer the composition, morphology and microstructure of the resultant M/NeC materials [20e26]. Among the studied precursors, MOFs constitute a fascinating class of self-sacrificed precursors/templates towards highly efficient M/NeC electrocatalysts due to their intrinsic advantages such as ultrahigh surface area, tunable pores/structures, and diversified compositions. Besides direct use of MOFs as the precursors, integration of MOFs with other precursors such as heteroatom-containing molecules (e.g. melamine and urea) or conductive carbon materials (e.g. nanotube and graphene) through varied methods (e.g. surface functionalization and cageencapsulation) have been also extensively investigated [27,28], which help further tune both active sites and the carbon structure indispensable for efficient ORR. A large volume of research in this area have revealed that the identity of transition metal has a profound impact on the electrocatalytic performance with these M/ NeC materials due to the fact that the specific electronic and geometric structure around each different transition metal may lead to
NeC composite electrocatalysts towards efficient electroreduction of j.electacta.2019.135273
distinct binding strength towards various intermediates in these electrochemical reactions [29,30]. For example, Fe or Co/NeC materials have been identified as the most promising ORR electrocatalysts to replace the benchmark Pt/C catalyst [31e35], whereas Ni/NeC counterparts have been recognized as the most competitive CO2RR electrocatalysts [36,37].
Compared to the extensively studied Fe, Co and Ni, copper (Cu), an earth-abundant element, is unique in some aspects. It has multiple easy-tuning valences (e.g. Cu (0), Cu (I), Cu (II) even Cu (III)), an outstanding water stability as well as an excellent electronic conductivity (only after Ag), all of which render it compatible with different redox reactions. In fact, trinuclear-copper-based laccase in biological system can realize a facile ORR process near the equilibrium potential [38]. Meanwhile, theoretical calculations have also pointed out that Cu situates close to the top of volcanoplot [39], which predicts a comparable ORR activity to the champion Pt catalyst. Encouraged by these facts and theoretical predictions, Cu and N-co-doped carbon-based ORR electrocatalysts have been actively explored, and various copper-relevant active sites have been proposed such as Cu(II)-Nx [40], Cu(I)-Nx [41], Cu@NeC [42] and Cu(0)-Cu(II)-Nx [43,44]. Amongst these active sites, Cu(0)-Cu(II)-Nx active site is quite special in terms of its configuration, in which not only the N atoms (e.g pyridinic-N) but also the Cu (0) atoms (e.g. metallic Cu NPs) can donate the free electrons to the d orbitals of Cu (II) ions, synergistically making a preferable binding between O2 and Cu (II) ions. Furthermore, nanosized Cu NPs and its alloys have been known for selective CO2RR to HCOOH, CO, CH4, even to C2H4 and C2H6 with relatively high efficiency [45,46]. With these in mind, it occurs to us that Cu(0)-Cu(II)-Nx active site actually makes a perfect combination of CO2RR-active Cu NPs and ORR-active Cu(II)-Nx sites, which is supposed to endow the catalysts with electrochemical bifunction towards ORR and CO2RR. In particular, the synergistic interactions between Cu NPs and its coordinated Cu(II)-Nx active site should also exert a great impact on the CO2RR catalytic performance of Cu NPs.
In this contribution, we have prepared a Cu@CueNeC composite bifunctional electrocatalyst from ZIF-8 (ZIF¼ zeolitic imidazolate framework) precursor, which first encapsulates CuCl2 into its nanocage, and then form Cu(OH)2@ZIF-8 upon treatment with KOH. After high-temperature calcination, the resultant Cu(OH)2@ZIF-8 was transformed into Cu NPs and Cu-Nx embedded carbon materials, namely CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-x-T (x¼molar percentage of Cu, and T¼ pyrolysis temperature). The optimal CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-810%-1000 in a hollow polyhedral morphology exhibits a fascinating catalytic bifunction towards ORR and CO2RR. In alkaline solution, it exhibits an ORR performance (E1/2¼ 0.83 V vs RHE) comparable to Pt/C (E1/2¼ 0.85 V vs RHE), proceeding in a near four-electron reduction mechanism. The primary Zn-air battery assembled with CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 as the cathode catalyst delivers a maximum power density of 116 mW cm 2, and the open circuit voltage (1.23 V) of Zn-air battery decays only by ca. 4.2% in 80 h at 20mA cm 2. At the same time, it also shows an outstanding CO2RR activity, selectively converting CO2 into CO with a high Faradaic efficiency (90% at 0.5 V vs RHE).

sections.heading: 2.1. Synthesis of ZIF-8
sections.text:
To synthesize ZIF-8 about 50 nm in size, 0.196mol of 2- methylimidazole in 480mL of methanol was added to 480mL of methanol containing 0.028mol of Zn(NO3)2$6H2O under vigorously stirring for 24 h at room temperature. The white precipitate was collected by centrifugation and washing for several times by

methanol, which was then thoroughly refluxed with methanol, followed by drying under vacuum at 65 C overnight. The ZIF-8 powder was further activated at 200 C under vacuum for 2 h prior to use.

sections.heading: 2.2. Synthesis of CuCl2@ZIF-8-x
sections.text: Typically, 0.87mmol of as-synthesized ZIF-8 was dispersed in 40mL of methanol by sonication for 0.5 h at room temperature, and then CuCl2$2H2O of various molars (x¼ 5%, 8%, 10%, 12%) (x represents the molar ratio of CuCl2$2H2O/(CuCl2$2H2O þ ZIF-8)) was subsequently added to the homogeneous solution under vigorous stirring for 12 h at room temperature, followed by centrifugation and washing with methanol for one time and drying in oven at 60 C overnight. The final power was denoted as CuCl2@ZIF-8-x.

sections.heading: 2.3. Synthesis of Cu(OH)2@ZIF-8-x
sections.text:
To the dried CuCl2@ZIF-8-x samples, 0.21mmol of KOH in 50mL of methanol solution was introduced during the vigorous stirring under room temperature to afford Cu(OH)2@ZIF-8-x. After 12 h, Cu(OH)2@ZIF-8-x was collected by centrifugation, followed by washing with methanol for three times and dried in a vacuum.
2.4. Synthesis of CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-x-T
CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-x-T are prepared as follows (T¼ pyrolysis temperature): the as-prepared Cu(OH)2@ZIF-8-x crystal precursors were placed in a ceramic boat and transferred into a temperature programmed furnace. The pyrolysis treatment was performed from 400 to 1000 C for 2 h with a heating rate of 5 C min 1 under N2 atmosphere. After cooling down to room temperature of furnace, the CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-T were obtained. The best ORR electrocatalytic performance was achieved by CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%1000 (vide infra). For comparison, C-ZIF-8-1000 were pyrolyzed from ZIF-8 in a similar procedure.

sections.heading: 2.5. Characterization and instrumentation
sections.text: Catalyst morphology was studied using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) on a Hitachi S-4800 system. Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) and High-Resolution Transmission Electron Microscopy (HRTEM) images were acquired by using a JEOL JEM 2100 F field emission electron microscope. The crystal phases present in each sample were identified using powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) (Ultima IV, Rigaku Corporation) with Cu K-a X-rays (l¼ 1.54056 Å). Nitrogen adsorption/desorption was investigated by a Micromeritics ASAP 2020 surface area. Raman spectra were recorded on a Thermo DXR 532 Raman spectrometer (USA) with a laser excitation wavelength of 532 nm. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) were performed using a Thermo Scientific Spectrometer with an Escalab 250 Xi X-ray as the excitation source, referenced to C 1s binding energy (BE) of 284.45 eV, and all samples were prepared as pressed powders supported on ametal bar for the XPS measurements. The contents of Cu were quantified by ICP-AES (inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscope) on a PerkinElmer Optima 3300DV ICP instrument.

sections.heading: 2.7. Zn-air battery test
sections.text:
The home-made Zn-air battery device was designed for the performance and stability test under ambient conditions. The catalyst ink was prepared by mixing 75mg of CeCu(OH)2-ZIF-810%-1000 with 1.2 g of a 5wt% Nafion solution and 3.5mL of IPA (nominal amount of solid Nafion of 45wt%). Then the ink treated by ultrasonication for 1 h. Finally, 100 mL of the ink was dropped on the carbon paper (1 cm 1 cm) with the catalyst loading amount of 1.0mg cm 2 and dried at room temperature. For the primary cells, a carbon paper electrode loaded with CeCu(OH)2-ZIF-8-10%-1000

sections.heading: 2.8. Electrochemical measurements and products analysis of the CO2RR
sections.text: All the electrochemical measurements of the CO2RR were carried out in a gas-tight two-component cell (separated by Nafion 115) with three-electrode system. Pt mesh and Ag/AgCl electrode (with saturated KCl as the filling solution) were used as the counter electrode and the reference electrode, respectively. The working electrode was prepared by dropping the catalyst ink (10mgmL 1) onto the carbon paper (Toray TGP-H-060, Toray Industries Inc.) at room temperature, giving a catalyst loading of 0.4mg cm 2. The area of theworking electrode is fixed at 0.5 cm2. The electrolytewas CO2-saturated 0.5M KHCO3 aqueous solution (pH was calibrated to the value of 7.2). All the potentials for CO2 reductionweremeasured against the Ag/AgCl electrode and converted to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) scale by E (vs. RHE) ¼ E (vs. Ag/AgCl) þ 0.197 Vþ 0.0591 pH. Prior to the controlled potential electrolysis, the electrolyte of two compartments was saturated with CO2 by bubbling CO2 gas for 30min. The electrolyte in the cathodic compartment was stirred at a rate of 500 rpm. During the electrolysis, CO2 gas was delivered at a rate of 20.00 standard cubic centimeters per minute (sccm) and routed directly into an on-line gas chromatograph (GC-2014, Shimadzu) equipped with FID and TCD detectors. The gas phase composition was analyzed by GC2014 every 10min. The Faradaic efficiencies and partial current densities for gas products are calculated as the previous work [47e51]. Liquid products were detected by 500MHz Bruker Avance-III NMR Spectrometer.

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussion
sections.text:
3.1. Synthesis and characterization of CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-T electrocatalyst
Two reports in literatures have described the preparation of ZIF8-derived Cu, N-co-doped carbon electrocatalysts (Cu/NeC) towards ORR, both involving the formation of Cu, Zn-bimetallic ZIF. In one report [33], Cu2þwas directly introduced into the framework of ZIF-8 by mixing Cu2þ, Zn2þ and 2-imidazole in one-pot reaction, forming Cu, Zn-bimetallic ZIF. In the other report [31], Cu, Znbimetallic ZIF was obtained by reaction of Zn2þ and 2-imidazole in the presence of Cu nanowires, which gradually turns into Cu2þ
under the reaction condition. In the current work, we adopted a different approach from these reports (Scheme 1). CuCl2 was encapsulated into the cavity of ZIF-8 through a wet impregnation method followed by treatment with the KOH solution, generating Cu(OH)2@ZIF-8-x (x¼ 5%, 8%, 10%, 12%). Eventually, the resultant Cu(OH)2@ZIF-8-x was subjected to calcination at different temperatures under the N2 atmosphere, giving CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-x-T (T represents pyrolysis temperature). During the calcination, the formed Cu(OH)2 is supposed to experience dehydration with the increasing temperature, evolving from the CuO through the Cu2O/ CuO mixed phase to the pure Cu2O phase (>800 C) (Fig. S1). The finally resulted Cu2O not only serves as the Cu source but also a template tuning the morphology, which can etch the carbonmatrix through the carbothermal reduction at the temperature above 800 C (Fig. S2 equation (3)). Among the CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-x-T catalysts, CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 delivers the best electrocatalytic performance (vide infra). Notably, CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-
NeC composite electrocatalysts towards efficient electroreduction of j.electacta.2019.135273
Scheme 1. Schematic showing of evolution from ZIF-8 to CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000.
1000 features a hollow rather than solid polyhedron morphology [33,34], which is obviously attributed to the different catalyst preparation method.
The PXRD pattern of Cu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10% is the same as ZIF-8, suggesting that framework structure of ZIF-8 is maintained (Fig. S3). SEM and TEM images further confirm that Cu(OH)2@ZIF8-10% well inherits the polyhedron shape of ZIF-8 (Fig. 1aeb and Figs. S4aeb). However, a different morphology was observed
Please cite this article as: X.-L. Chen et al., ZIF-derived bifunctional Cu@Cue oxygen and carbon dioxide, Electrochimica Acta, https://doi.org/10.1016/
between CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 and C-ZIF-8-1000 (Fig. 1c and Fig. S4c). C-ZIF-8-1000 remains the solid polyhedron morphology but with a rough surface. In sharp contrast, CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 represents a hollow polyhedral structure defined by light interior and dark edge (c.a. 5 nm thick Fig. S5). Although PXRD pattern of CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-10%-1000 manifests the diffraction peaks of metallic Cu NPs (PDF#04e0836) (Fig. S6), none of them are spotted in TEM pictures of different
Cu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 (c); (d) HADDF-STEM image and the corresponding element

regions more probably because the Cu nanoparticles are well dispersed within the carbon matrix. HAADF-STEM images of CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 coupled with the element mapping indicates that C, N and Cu elements are well dispersed within the entire carbon matrix (Fig. 1d).
To better understand the formation process of CeCu(OH)2@ZIF8-10%-1000, the transition of Cu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10% with the temperature (T¼ 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900 and 1000 C) was tracked by IR, PXRD, as well as TEM (Fig. 2). FT-IR spectra of CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-T demonstrate that the well-defined vibration profile of ZIF-8 is still kept at 400 C, and above 400 C only some broad bands are left (Fig. 2a). Complying with the FT-IR change, PXRD pattern at 400 C is almost identical with ZIF-8, which completely disappears at 500 C concurrent with the generation of strong and sharp signals of ZnO (PDF#36e1451). From 500 C to 700 C, PXRD patterns are almost the same but the intensity of ZnO peaks obviously decreases with the rising
temperature. At 800 C, the ZnO signals are totally invisible with the simultaneous formation of metallic Cu (PDF#04e0836) and graphitic carbon peaks (2qz 24.0 and 43.0 ), both of which show a gradual increase in intensity from 800 C to 1000 C (Fig. 2b). TEM images of CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-T offer a direct visualization of the change in the solid polyhedral morphology of ZIF-8 (Fig. 2ceh). It clearly shows that the morphology change occurs at 800 C, at which the initial solid polyhedron turns into a hollow one. According to the above data, the hollow polyhedron formation is proposed as follows. At 500 C, reaction of Zn2þ in ZIF-8 with OH
from Cu(OH)2 generates Zn(OH)2 followed by the decomposition into ZnO with the rising temperature, which also destructs the framework of ZIF-8. From 500 to 700 C, the decreasing ZnO is probably caused by reduction of H2 which comes from dehydrogenation of ZIF-8 during the calcination [52]. Meanwhile, the initial Cu(OH)2 also undergoes the transformation from CuO through the mixed CuO/Cu2O to Cu2O with the rising temperature (Fig. S1).
700, 800, 900 and 1000 C) tracked by IR (a), PXRD (b), as well as TEM (ceh).
When the temperature reaches 800 C, carbothermal reduction between ZnO/Cu2O with carbon is initiated with simultaneous release of CO gas [53,54], which is responsible for the formation of hollow structure.
Similar to C-ZIF-8-1000, Raman spectra of CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-810%-1000 displays two characteristic peaks at 1350 cm 1 and 1585 cm 1 corresponding to the vibrations of the disordered carbon and the graphitic carbon. Nonetheless, the ID/IG with CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 (0.98) is evidently larger than C-ZIF8-1000 (0.91), inferring the presence of more structure effects (Fig. S7). N2 absorption-desorption isotherms reveal that CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 has a much larger Brunauer-EmmettTeller (BET) surface area (1184.2m2/g) than C-ZIF-8-1000 (785.6m2/g) and more abundant mesopores (Fig. S8).
XPS spectra uncover the composition and chemical state of elements at the surface of carbon electrocatalysts. Comparison of the XPS survey spectra between CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 and CZIF-8-1000 confirm that the Cu element has been successfully doped into CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 along with C, N and O elements (Fig. 3a). High-resolution of Cu2p XPS spectra further disclose that the surficial Cu element of CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%1000 exists in multiple valences including Cu (0)/(I) and Cu (II) (Fig. 3b). The detection of Cu (0) species agree well with the observation of PXRD peaks of metallic copper in CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-810%-1000. The Cu (I) and Cu (II) species might coordinate the doped
N atoms to generate Cu (I/II)-Nx active sites, which is also collaborated by high-resolution N1s XPS spectra comprising five subpeaks, viz. pyridinic-N (398.40 eV), Cu(II)-Nx (399.01 eV), pyrrolicN (400.01eV), graphitic-N (401.02eV) and oxidized-N (402.98eV) (Fig. 3c). The impact of temperature on N1s XPS spectra of CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-T (T¼ 700, 800, 900 and 1000 C) has also been scrutinized (Fig. 3d). It is found that the Cu-Nx active sites are only formed above 800 C and increase in intensity with the rising temperature. Given that the morphology transition also occurs at the turning temperature of 800 C (Fig. 2), it can be reasonably concluded that the Cu-Nx active sites are created by carbothermal reduction between Cu2O and carbon.

sections.heading: 3.2. Electrochemical reduction of oxygen
sections.text:
The ORR activity of CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-x-T catalysts were evaluated using LSV measurement in 0.1M O2-saturated KOH solution, and the best ORR performance was found with CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-810%-1000 (Fig. S9). Compared to C-ZIF-8-1000 (Eonset¼ 0.86 V; E1/ 2¼ 0.76 V), CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 shows a more positive onset potential (Eonset) of 0.93 V (vs. RHE) and half-wave potential (E1/2) of 0.83 V (vs. RHE) comparable to the benchmark Pt/C (Eonset¼ 1.01 V; E1/2¼ 0.85 V) (Fig. 4a). It is noteworthy that CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 also ranks as one of the best Cu, N-codoped carbon electrocatalysts towards ORR (Table S1). RRDE test

Fig. 4. (a) LSV curves for C-ZIF-8-1000, CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 and Pt/C in O2-saturated 0.1M KOH solutions with a rotation speed of 1600 rpm and a sweep rate of 10mV s 1; (b) Percentage of peroxide and electron transfer numbers of CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 in O2-saturated 0.1M KOH electrolyte; (c) Polarization and corresponding power density curves of the primary Zneair battery based on CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 and Pt/C. (d) Discharge curves of a Zneair battery assembled from CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 catalysts at a current density of 20mA cm 2 (inset: Photograph of the zinceair battery displaying a measured open circuit voltage of a lighted LED).

The electron transfer number (n) of CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 measured by RRDE is also in accordance with the value (n¼ 3.5) calculated using the Koutecky-Levich (K-L) equation on the basis of K-L plots (j 1 vs u 1/2) (Fig. S10). Except the excellent ORR activity and selectivity, CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 also demonstrates a good methanol tolerance and long-term durability. The CV curve of CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 in alkaline electrolyte almost remains intact upon addition of methanol (Fig. S11), and accelerated duration test (ADT) only shows a minor loss of 6mV in E1/2 after 10 000 cycles (Fig. S12).
To gain more insight into the active sites in CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-810%-1000, two control experiments have been carried out. In one experiment, 1,10-Phenanthroline (Phen) as the probe for Cu-Nx active site was added into the alkaline electrolyte. Upon addition of Phen, a striking negative shift (△E1/2¼ 56mV) in E1/2 was observed (Fig. S13), suggesting the existence and the crucial role of Cu-Nx in CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000. Similarly, the inhibition effect of Phen towards ORR activity was also noticed with CeCu(OH)2@ZIF8-10%-800 (△E1/2¼ 30mV) and CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-900 (△E1/ 2¼ 41mV) (Fig. S13). It can be clearly seen that the inhibition strength of Phen measured by △E1/2 increases with the increasing intensity of Cu-Nx active sites of CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-T ((T¼ 800, 900, 1000 C). Thereby, the effect of calcination temperature on ORR activity of CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-T (T¼ 800, 900, 1000 C) might be partially attributed to the temperature-dependent
Please cite this article as: X.-L. Chen et al., ZIF-derived bifunctional Cu@Cue oxygen and carbon dioxide, Electrochimica Acta, https://doi.org/10.1016/
number of Cu-Nx active sites. In another experiment, CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 was thoroughly stirred with 0.5M HNO3 solution at 80 C for 12 h to remove the metallic Cu nanoparticles, and then subjected to ORR test. A remarkable drop in ORR performance (△E1/2¼ 40mV) was resulted with the acid-etching catalyst (herein referred as CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000-AT) (Fig. S14), inferring the significance of metallic Cu NPs for oxygen reduction either in the form of Cu@NeC or Cu(0)-Cu(II)-Nx. The acid-etching treatment not only removes the Cu NPs but also destroys the associated Cu(II)-Nx active sites, thus lowering the ORR activity [33,34]. Moreover, a reduction in electronic conduction due to the removal of highly electron-conducting Cu NPs was also observed in the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) of CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-%-1000-AT compared to CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8%-1000 (Fig. S15), which also partly accounts for the degraded ORR activity as the result of increasing electron-transfer resistance.

sections.heading: 3.3. Performance evaluation of Zn-air battery
sections.text:
Thanks to their high theoretical energy density, environmentalfriendliness, affordability, and safety, Zn-air batteries have attracted extensive attention as promising energy storage devices [55,56]. However, there remains great challenges in the development of active and durable ORR electrocatalysts used in Zn-air batteries. In this context, ZIF-8 derived transition metal (M¼ Fe, Co etc) and nitrogen (N) co-doped carbon materials has emerged as promising electrode materials in Zn-air batteries largely because of the intrinsic advantages with ZIF-8 such as excellent thermal stability,
NeC composite electrocatalysts towards efficient electroreduction of j.electacta.2019.135273
high N-content ligands, as well as easy evaporation of Zn atoms at above 900 C [57]. These materials typically show well-defined Ndoped carbon skeletons with homogenous porous texture which is supposed to facilitate mass transport and generate high power density in Zn-air battery tests. Although Fe or Co and N co-doped carbon materials have been successfully applied as cathode ORR electrocatalysts in Zn-air batteries but the long-term duration of thesematerials still need to be further improved. To our knowledge, Cu, N-co-doped carbon electrocatalyst have been reported as promising ORR electrocatalysts but less investigated in the Zn-air batteries [34,58]. Nonetheless, the strong CueN coordination bond along with the outstanding water stability of copper might convey the long-term stability into these Cu, N-co-doped carbon materials whenworking in the Zn-air batteries. With these inmind, the highly active and stable CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 catalyst was then applied as a cathode catalyst in a homemade Zinceair battery. The polarization and power density curves show that the Zinceair battery assembled from CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 exhibited an open-circuit voltage of 1.230 V and a maximal power density of 116mWcm 2 at 156mA cm 2, which is much higher than those of Pt/C (~1.176 V and ~80mWcm 2 at 166mA cm 2) (Fig. 4c). Notably, only 4.2% of output voltage was lost at 20mA cm 2 for 80 h (Fig. 4d), again accentuating its prominent durability. The outstanding catalytic performance of CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 can be attributed to well-distributed Cu-Nx active sites, the enhanced electrical conductivity tuned by metal Cu NPs, and hollow carbon nanostructures with large surface area. The excellent stability of CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 is assumed to be an outstandingwater stability with copper as well as strong and stable Cu-Nx bonds [59].
Please cite this article as: X.-L. Chen et al., ZIF-derived bifunctional Cu@Cue oxygen and carbon dioxide, Electrochimica Acta, https://doi.org/10.1016/

sections.heading: 3.4. Electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide
sections.text:
The electrocatalytic activity of CO2 reduction on CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 was evaluated by LSV in CO2-saturated 0.5M KHCO3 solution with the reference to C-ZIF-8-1000. As depicted in Fig. 5a, CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 catalyst exhibits the onset potential of 0.35 V (vs. RHE), which is more positive than that of C-ZIF-8-1000 ( 0.6 V). Meanwhile, a higher current density is reached on CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 than C-ZIF-81000 (Fig. 5a and Fig. S16). Further, controlled potential electrolysis was carried out to measure the activity and selectivity by combining products quantitative analysis (Fig. S16). The primary reduction products are CO and H2 authenticated by online GC, and there is no liquid product detected by 1H nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (Fig. S17). The CO Faradaic efficiency (FE) on CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 varies from 75% to 90% over the potential range of 0.40 ~ 0.70 V, and the maximum FE is achieved at 0.50 V which is almost 3-fold higher than C-ZIF-8-1000 (35.2%) (Fig. 5b). To our knowledge, CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 constitutes a rare example of Cu, N-codoped carbon electrocatalysts towards efficient CO2RR. Further control experiments have proved that metallic Cu nanoparticles and Cu-Nx are both indispensable for acquiring the excellent CO2RR performance on CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-810%-1000 (Fig. 5c and d). On the one hand, the concurrent decay of CO2RR activity and selectivity occurs on CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%1000-AT, suggesting the crucial role of Cu NPs for CO2RR. On the other hand, the addition of Phen significantly decreases the catalytic activity of CeCu(OH)2@ZIF-8-10%-1000 but exerts a minor effect on CO selectivity, inferring that some Cu-Nx active sites link to Cu NPs just like Cu(0)-Cu(II)-Nx, presenting a synergistic effect.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
A Cu@CueNeC composite electrocatalyst was fabricated from Cu(OH)2@ZIF-8, wherein the encapsulated Cu(OH)2 gradually transforms into the final Cu2Owith the increasing temperature. The Cu@CueNeC catalyst shows a hollow polyhedral morphology which is created by carbothermal reduction of in-situ formed Cu2O and ZnO with carbon beyond 800 C. An impressive bifunctional catalytic activity towards both ORR and CO2RR is found with these Cu@CueNeC composite electrocatalysts due to the presence of Cu(0)-Cu(II)-Nx active sites. More importantly, the current work demonstrates that the synergistic interactions between Cu (0) and Cu(II)-Nx are beneficial to attain high ORR and CO2RR performance.
